memory_candidates.content: When a shell-test-suite timing assertion measures wall-clock elapsed time (e.g. 'parallel run finishes under N ms'), an ABSOLUTE millisecond threshold is not robust on a shared development machine: unrelated concurrent processes (other agent sessions, builds, pytest runs) can inflate wall-clock measurements by 2-3x transiently, causing a correct implementation to flake. The fix is a RELATIVE ratio: measure the two conditions being compared (e.g. parallel vs. forced-sequential) back-to-back in the same test run, and assert a ratio between them (e.g. parallel_ms <= 75% of sequential_ms) rather than either an absolute ceiling or floor. An external load multiplier inflates both measurements roughly proportionally, so the ratio stays meaningful regardless of host load, while a genuine regression (e.g. parallelism silently becoming a no-op) still fails the ratio check reliably. Diagnosed by first (incorrectly) hypothesizing sibling-test contention within the same test runner's own concurrency pool, then falsifying that hypothesis by observing the flake persisted even when the suite was serialized/isolated from siblings -- the real cause was external, machine-wide load, confirmed via free -h/ps aux showing heavy swap usage from unrelated sessions.

When adding an opt-in gate-selection or scope-reduction flag to a verifier/battery script (e.g. --only-gate N to skip N-1 of N checks), do a full cross-check-variable dependency audit BEFORE wiring the guard -- read every check block and confirm no later check reads a variable an earlier, now-skippable check assigns. If the audit finds zero cross-dependencies (common when each check is written as a self-contained block with uniquely-named local variables), the guard can be added mechanically (wrap each block in 'if selected(N); then ... fi' without reindenting the body) with high confidence and a small, reviewable diff. Verify empirically too: run every individual selection standalone and confirm none crashes with an unbound-variable or unset-path error -- this is the regression net for the audit's own correctness.

In a source-store-to-deploy architecture (edits land in a source tree, a separate 'deploy' step syncs them to a consumed/deployed copy), a self-verifying deploy-drift gate (checking deployed content == source content) will correctly flag ANY in-flight, uncommitted-to-deploy edit as drift -- including your own current task's edits, and any concurrently-scheduled sibling task's edits, for as long as redeploy is deliberately deferred to a later phase. This is expected and NOT a regression: confirm by git-stashing your own edit and re-running the check (if it passes clean, the drift was self-caused); if it still fails with your edit stashed, another in-flight file is the cause (check via a direct fixture rebuild + verifier run, since stashing stops being useful once your own earlier-phase edits are committed to source history rather than just working-tree diffs).
